claims.text: Conventionally cast high-entropy alloys have coarse grains and limited microstructural refinement.
Cyclic rapid solidification followed by controlled aging will produce a dual-phase or fine precipitate-dispersed microstructure in high-entropy alloys.
Quench rates from 10^2 to 10^5 K/s constitute an effective processing range for the proposed treatment.
Aging temperatures from 500°C to 800°C constitute an effective processing range for the proposed treatment.
A controlled atmosphere will help ensure reproducible quench rates and aging profiles.
Rapid solidification creates a non-equilibrium structure in the alloy.
Controlled aging permits fine-tuning of precipitate formation.
Controlled aging after rapid solidification permits further grain refinement.
The tailored dual-phase or precipitate-dispersed microstructure enhances work hardening.
The tailored microstructure delays crack initiation.
Microstructural tailoring can overcome the usual strength-ductility trade-off.
The treated alloys will have higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths than conventionally cast state-of-the-art alloys.
The treated alloys will have greater tensile elongation than conventionally cast state-of-the-art alloys.
The treated alloys will have an elevated or otherwise optimized Young's modulus.
The treated alloys will have greater fracture toughness than conventionally cast state-of-the-art alloys.
Cooling rates below the proposed window or excessively high aging temperatures may prevent formation of the desired microstructure or degrade mechanical performance.
The effect is alloy-specific and may not persist under service conditions beyond ambient or moderately elevated temperatures.
Prior evidence shows that thermal and thermomechanical treatments can beneficially alter high-entropy-alloy microstructures.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in all four targeted properties, or failure to observe the anticipated microstructure, is proposed as a falsification criterion.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says Young's modulus will be elevated, whereas the predicted outcome permits an undefined 'more favorable (or optimized)' modulus and the falsification rule merely requires an improvement. The direction and meaning of the modulus target are therefore inconsistent or ambiguous.
